questions.title: Jones major criterion — the exclusion
questions.question: Jones major criteria for diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever does not include:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sydenham chorea is one of the five Jones MAJOR criteria, so it is included.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Carditis is a Jones MAJOR criterion, so it is included.
explanations.C: Correct. ARTHRALGIA (joint pain without objective signs of inflammation) is a MINOR criterion, not a major one, so it is the item NOT included among the majors. The five Jones MAJOR criteria are carditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum. The minor criteria include arthralgia, fever, raised acute-phase reactants and a prolonged PR interval.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Subcutaneous nodules are a Jones MAJOR criterion, so they are included.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the Jones major criteria (arthritis) from the minor criteria (arthralgia).

questions.title: Where the Aschoff nodule is best seen
questions.question: Aschoff's nodule in rheumatic heart is best seen in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The valves show the warty rheumatic vegetations and later fibrous fusion, but the diagnostic Aschoff nodule is not best seen there.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The endocardium (including MacCallum's patch) is involved, but the Aschoff nodule is characteristically a myocardial lesion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pericardium shows serofibrinous ('bread-and-butter') pericarditis, not the Aschoff nodule.
explanations.D: Correct. Although rheumatic fever is a PANCARDITIS, the pathognomonic ASCHOFF NODULE is best seen in the MYOCARDIUM, characteristically in the perivascular interstitial connective tissue. It shows central fibrinoid necrosis ringed by activated macrophages (Anitschkow cells), multinucleate Aschoff giant cells and lymphocytes. This myocardial interstitial location is where the diagnostic lesion is identified.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Aschoff nodule is best seen in the myocardium (perivascular interstitium).

questions.title: Bread-and-butter pericardium indicates
questions.question: Bread and butter appearance of pericardium in rheumatic fever indicates:

explanations.A: Correct. The 'BREAD-AND-BUTTER' appearance is the gross hallmark of SEROFIBRINOUS (fibrinous) pericarditis: a fibrin-rich exudate coats the visceral and parietal pericardial surfaces, and pulling the inflamed layers apart draws out shaggy fibrin strands like buttered bread being separated. This is the characteristic rheumatic pericarditis. It usually resolves without significant constriction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Haemorrhagic pericarditis (blood-stained exudate) suggests tuberculosis or malignancy, not the fibrinous rheumatic pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Suppurative (purulent) pericarditis is caused by pyogenic bacteria, not rheumatic fever.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Constrictive pericarditis is a late fibrosing/calcifying sequel, not the acute bread-and-butter appearance.

questions.learning_objective: Link the bread-and-butter pericardium to serofibrinous pericarditis of rheumatic fever.

questions.title: Acute infective endocarditis — the false feature
questions.question: Acute infective endocarditis does not have the following feature:

options.A: Caused by a highly virulent organism, e.g. Staphylococcus aureus
options.B: Affects a previously injured or abnormal valve
options.C: The larger vegetation often causes embolic complication
options.D: Death occurs in days to weeks in 50 to 60% of the patients

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true feature). Acute infective endocarditis is caused by highly virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus.
explanations.B: Correct (the feature it does NOT have). Acute infective endocarditis characteristically attacks PREVIOUSLY NORMAL (healthy) valves, destroying them rapidly. Affecting an already injured or abnormal valve describes the SUBACUTE form, in which low-virulence organisms seed damaged valves. Therefore 'affects a previously injured valve' is not a feature of the acute form and is the answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true feature). The large septic vegetations of acute infective endocarditis frequently break off to cause embolic complications and septic infarcts.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a true feature). Acute infective endocarditis is rapidly progressive and fatal in a high proportion (about 50-60%) of patients within days to weeks.

questions.learning_objective: State that acute infective endocarditis attacks previously normal valves (subacute affects damaged valves).

questions.title: Characteristic histologic feature of rheumatic fever
questions.question: The characteristic histologic feature of rheumatic fever is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The rheumatoid nodule is the lesion of rheumatoid arthritis, not rheumatic fever.
explanations.B: Correct. The ASCHOFF NODULE (body) is the characteristic (pathognomonic) HISTOLOGIC lesion of rheumatic fever: a focus of central fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by activated macrophages (Anitschkow cells with 'caterpillar' chromatin), multinucleate Aschoff giant cells, lymphocytes and plasma cells. It is found chiefly in the myocardial interstitium. Its presence is diagnostic of rheumatic carditis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. MacCallum's patch is a GROSS lesion (subendocardial thickening of the left atrium), not the characteristic histologic feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peyer's patches are normal gut-associated lymphoid tissue and are unrelated to rheumatic fever.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Aschoff nodule as the characteristic histologic lesion of rheumatic fever.

questions.title: Site of MacCallum's patch (healed rheumatic endocarditis)
questions.question: MacCallum's patch is healed rheumatic endocarditis in:

options.A: The posterior wall of the right atrium
options.B: The posterior wall of the right ventricle
options.C: The posterior wall of the left atrium
options.D: The posterior wall of the left ventricle

explanations.A: Incorrect. MacCallum's patch is a left-sided, not right-atrial, lesion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The right ventricle is not the site of MacCallum's patch.
explanations.C: Correct. MacCALLUM'S PATCH is a map-like area of subendocardial thickening (healed rheumatic endocarditis) on the POSTERIOR WALL of the LEFT ATRIUM. It results from friction and the regurgitant jet across the inflamed mitral valve, producing subendocardial fibrosis at that site. Its left-atrial posterior-wall location is the specific fact tested.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Although the left ventricle is on the mitral side, the patch classically lies on the posterior wall of the left ATRIUM, above the mitral valve.

questions.learning_objective: State that MacCallum's patch (healed rheumatic endocarditis) lies on the posterior wall of the left atrium.

questions.title: Subacute infective endocarditis — the false feature
questions.question: The following are characteristic of subacute infective endocarditis except:

options.A: Common in mitral and aortic valve

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true feature). Subacute infective endocarditis characteristically affects the left-sided mitral and aortic valves, which are the valves most often previously damaged.
explanations.B: Incorrect (a true feature). The subacute form produces large, bulky, brownish but relatively non-destructive vegetations.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true feature). Because low-virulence organisms drive an indolent course, few or no pus cells are seen microscopically in the subacute form.
explanations.D: Correct (the false feature). Friable vegetations with VALVE PERFORATION and rapid destruction are features of ACUTE infective endocarditis by virulent organisms, NOT of the subacute form. The subacute form is comparatively non-destructive and does not perforate the valve. Therefore this is the exception among the listed features.

questions.learning_objective: State that valve perforation/destructive friable vegetations belong to acute, not subacute, infective endocarditis.
